posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a round, fluffy dark brown Shetland pony with a cream forelock peering over the edge of a water trough at his own reflection in a green pasture. Text at the top reads: Field report: there's another pony in the water trough. He's my exact size. I've told him the hay is mine.
posts.caption: The pony in our back pasture found the water trough this week, and I mean really found it. I came out with the wheelbarrow at 7:30 and he was standing over it, perfectly still, studying the surface like it owed him money. Every so often he'd lift one hoof and set it down again, very gently, as though negotiating. The barn cat sat on the fence post watching the whole thing with her tail wrapped around her feet. It went on for twenty minutes. I refilled the trough around him. He didn't blink, and I'm fairly sure he won.
posts.first: My first pony did something similar with a rain puddle in the driveway. He stood over it for an entire lesson while my instructor explained, calmly, that horses cannot be reasoned with before breakfast. I was nine. I remember agreeing completely. I still keep that rule on the tack room door.

posts.caption: Every barn has someone who remembers how it used to be, and ours is the gray gelding in the end stall. He came to us at nineteen with a bad hock and strong opinions about sweet feed. This week I found him at his door at 4:30, a full hour early, ears forward, waiting on a sound he's heard thousands of times. I took my time getting the scoop. He stood there looking like a man waiting on a train that's never been late. I gave him extra. He accepted it as his due.
posts.first: My grandfather kept a cow bell on a nail by the kitchen door and rang it for supper every night of his life. We all came in at the first note, even the dogs. I think about that bell every time I rattle the scoop. Some sounds just mean home.

posts.caption: The saddle fitter drove ninety minutes with a truck full of saddles and a tape measure she held like a weapon. She walked around Red twice, put her hands on her withers, and said 'huh' in a tone I've heard from mechanics. Then came the shims, the pads, and three different trees. Red stood for all of it with one hoof up, offering notes. Two hours and a very nice invoice later, we have a saddle that fits. Red inspected it, sighed through her nose, and went back to her hay as though she'd arranged the whole thing.
posts.first: I rode in an ill-fitting saddle for most of my twenties and blamed my own posture every time. Nobody told me the saddle was allowed to be the problem. Red would have told me within a week. I think about those years whenever the fitter opens her truck.

posts.quote: The hay truck was promised for noon. It arrived at dusk, and we stacked it by headlight like we always do.
posts.first: Eleven years of hay deliveries, and the truck has never once arrived when it said it would. It has also never once failed to arrive. I stopped checking the clock around year three and started keeping a flashlight in the tack room. It's a good system, and nobody planned it.

posts.caption: The trail ride was a fundraiser for the pony club, with a map, a clipboard, and a volunteer in a bright orange vest at every turn. Everyone had been promised views. We did get views, mostly of the hill, and a long stretch of someone's hay field. The chestnut mare walked it with her head high like she was being photographed for a calendar. She stopped twice at the best light and waited. Nobody noticed. By the finish line she'd decided the volunteer in orange was part of the show, and gave him a nod.
posts.first: I rode that same trail on a borrowed gelding twenty years ago and was too nervous to notice a single leaf. This time the leaves were gold, the sky was the color of a warm pie crust, and the horse knew it. I think the view got better because I stopped bracing for it.

posts.caption: The shavings truck backed up to the barn at 8:20, and by 9:00 every stall in the aisle had a fresh bed, fluffed up like a hotel mattress. I do the last stall myself because the Homebody gets particular. She watched me from the doorway, then walked in, turned around twice, and lay down in the new shavings before I'd put the fork away. Her barn cat arrived thirty seconds later and settled on her hip. The two of them were asleep by the time I finished the aisle. I swept around them.
posts.first: I once bought a mattress that cost more than my first horse. I've never loved it the way she loves a bag of pine shavings. It makes me wonder what I've been spending money on. Then I think about my first horse, and I stop.
